title: Switching costs
hookLine: switching between tasks costs time and accuracy, even when it seems fast

lines: THREE TABS AND A BUZZING TEXT.
THE BILL ARRIVES IN SMALL COINS.
cards: Three tabs open. An email half written. A text that just buzzed.
A spreadsheet waiting underneath it all. A glance here, a reply there, back to the email, over to the sheet. To the person doing it, this can seem nimble, even fast.
Psychologists who study attention have a dry name for what all that hopping charges you: switching costs.
People asked to swap back and forth between two simple jobs get slower and make more mistakes than people who stay with one. And the charge is quiet. The switch seems instant.

teach.b: In a common kind of task-switching study, people see a number or a letter and make a quick judgment about it. Sometimes the rule stays the same from one trial to the next; sometimes it changes.
When it changes, answers come more slowly and with more errors. Researchers call that gap the switch cost. Why?
One explanation is that the mind has to put down one set of rules and pick up another, a kind of reloading.
A warning that a switch is coming makes the cost smaller, though in some studies a piece of it stays even when people know exactly what's next. Now an old letter.

The Roman philosopher Seneca, writing to his friend Lucilius about reading too many books and traveling too much, puts it in three words: "Everywhere means nowhere." He wasn't measuring reaction times.
He was describing a mind that never settles long enough to arrive. And an honest limit. Lab tasks are tiny, and a real workday is not a lab.

How much these small costs add up across an ordinary afternoon is still argued over, and researchers disagree about the size. The modest takeaway: each switch has some price, and some switches are worth paying for.
The ones that aren't are often small and automatic, like the glance at a message that could have waited an hour.

how: People who take task-switching research to heart often batch their email and messages into set times of day, and some contemplative teachers frame doing one thing at a time as a practice in its own right.

practice: Choose two times later today to check and answer your messages together, as a batch, and say them to yourself once.
Then make this sit a single task: rest on the breath, and each time attention jumps to a message, a plan or a noise, notice that it switched and come back, with no scorekeeping.

wordCard.voice: Switching costs. The time and accuracy lost when the mind changes from one task to another, even when the change seems quick. Today's word.

orig.note: Seneca's Latin, Letter 2: the one who is everywhere is nowhere.

carryVoice: Your line: one at a time. Seneca said it in three words: everywhere means nowhere. Until next time.
